questions.prompt: Walk through what happens when Morphic's research agent calls its fetch tool with a URL such as http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/: what checks the URL passes, where the request is made from, what can stop it, and what comes back into the model's context.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The URL is model-controlled and barely checked: the tool's schema accepts any string as url, with no URL shape, scheme or host rule.

[w3] With the default regular type the server itself fetches the URL from its own network, so a private address, localhost or a cloud metadata endpoint is reachable if the host can reach it; nothing in the code denies such ranges.
[w2] What does stop a request is incidental: a 10-second abort, a non-2xx status, or a content type that is neither text/html nor text/plain, so a plain-text internal endpoint passes.
[w2] The response body comes back as model context: scripts, styles and tags are stripped, and up to 50,000 characters of text plus the page title are returned as the tool result.
[w2] The api type moves the fetch off the server's network to Jina Reader or Tavily Extract, which removes the internal-network reach but hands the full URL, query string included, to a third party.
[w1] The only rule about when to fetch is in the system prompt (use fetch only for a URL the user gave), which steers the model but is not enforced by any code.

questions.prompt: Explain how text inside a fetched page can steer Morphic's next tool call, and which boundaries in this code could stop it at this commit.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Fetched text and the user's request reach the model through the same context, so instructions planted in a page can ask the agent to fetch another URL; the tool loop runs that call like any other.
[w2] The loop's reach is bounded only by its step budget: 20 steps in quick mode and 50 in adaptive mode, each of which may be another fetch.
[w2] Stripping scripts and tags removes markup, not instructions: any visible text, including text written for a model, survives into the tool result.

[w2] The search self-call is a second egress point: when no BASE_URL is configured, its target is built from request headers (x-base-url, x-url or x-host), and the proxy derives its own copy from x-forwarded-host, so whoever controls those headers can point the server's POST elsewhere.
[w2] No boundary in the tool code distinguishes a URL the user typed from one the model found; enforcing the prompt's rule would mean checking the URL against the user's message before fetching.
keyPoints.quote: Does any new code fetch a URL the user/model controls?

questions.prompt: Defend or indict the claim "network egress rules make Morphic's fetch tool safe": what would you verify before calling it a vulnerability, and what is the smallest code fix?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Egress rules help only where they exist: the code ships no denylist, so safety depends entirely on the deployment, and the checklist itself rates it as unresolved.

[w2] Before calling it a vulnerability, verify it on the real deployment: whether the host can reach metadata or internal addresses, and whether a guest can trigger it (guest chat is off unless ENABLE_GUEST_CHAT is true).

[w3] The smallest fix sits in fetchRegularData before the request: parse the URL, allow only http and https, resolve the host and refuse private, loopback, link-local and metadata ranges, and re-check after every redirect, since no redirect policy is set today.
[w2] A check on the host name alone is not enough: the name has to be resolved and the connection pinned to the checked address, or a DNS answer that changes between check and fetch slips through.
[w2] Tightening the schema helps the error, not the defence: z.string().url() would reject non-URLs early, but a well-formed internal URL still passes.
